Pick's Theorem

AreaCountingCoordinates
Game: Draw a shape with corners on the dots of a grid, and count the dots on its edge and inside it. The numbers tell its area.
How to play: Press dots to put the corners down one by one; the last one joins the first. Choose "Delete nodes" to take a corner away. Arrow keys and Enter work too.

Mode
Look for the math

Draw a shape whose corners are dots of a square grid and whose sides do not cross. Let B be the number of dots on its edge and I the number inside. Then its area is a very simple sum.

Pick's formula

Area = I + B/2 − 1

This is Pick's theorem, published by Georg Pick in 1899. A single unit square has B = 4 and I = 0, so the area is 0 + 2 − 1 = 1. A triangle with B = 3 and I = 0 has area 1/2, which is why some areas on this page end in ½.

Checked, not trusted

The test counted the dots on the edge two ways (testing every dot, and adding up the greatest common divisors of the steps along each side) and the dots inside by testing each one, for tens of thousands of random shapes on this board. The area from the formula equalled the area from the shoelace formula every time. Each side that goes a steps across and b up holds gcd(a, b) of the edge dots, which is why steep sides with a common factor add extra dots.

Why it is true

The proof cuts the shape into small triangles with no dot inside or on their sides except their corners, each of area 1/2, and counts them with Euler's formula: it gives 2I + B − 2 triangles. Pick's formula is in fact equivalent to Euler's formula.

Make a shape with no dots inside and a long thin side, such as one with corners at (1,1), (7,1) and (1,2). What does B tell you about the area?
